candidate_findings.message: On Android every non-seekable StreamMediaSource fails to open: the length calculation produces C.LengthUnset (-1), and the following `bytesRemaining < 0` guard then throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException, even though the code has a branch meant to support non-seekable streams. The constructor sets `length = stream.CanSeek ? stream.Length : C.LengthUnset`. In Open, `bytesRemaining = dataSpec.Length != C.LengthUnset ? dataSpec.Length : (length != C.LengthUnset ? length - dataSpec.Position : C.LengthUnset)` is -1 when both lengths are unset, which is the usual case for a progressive source. The next line is `if (bytesRemaining < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(...)`, so it throws. Trigger: `MediaElement.Source = MediaSource.FromStream(await httpClient.GetStreamAsync(url))` on Android. Even with the guard fixed, a second Open at position 0 after the extractor has sniffed the stream would read data the stream has already consumed.

On Windows, a non-seekable stream makes PlatformUpdateSource throw, because AsRandomAccessStream needs a seekable stream. Nothing documents that StreamMediaSource needs a seekable stream, and the platforms behave differently: Android throws, Windows throws, iOS reports a ContentLength of 0. `var randomAccessStream = streamMediaSource.Stream.AsRandomAccessStream();` has no CanSeek check and no try/catch. The StreamMediaSource XML docs (StreamMediaSource.shared.cs) only say "the stream to use as a media source" and say nothing about seekability or who owns the stream.

The iOS resource loader answers each data request with one read of the full requested length cast to int. A large request can overflow or allocate a huge buffer, and on any read error it still calls FinishLoading, so AVFoundation treats the empty response as success instead of a failure. `var requestedLength = (int)dataRequest.RequestedLength;` is followed by `var buffer = new byte[requestedLength]; stream.Read(buffer, 0, requestedLength)` (one Read call, no loop for short reads). The catch only does `Debug.WriteLine`. ShouldWaitForLoadingOfRequestedResource then calls `loadingRequest.FinishLoading()` unconditionally rather than `FinishLoadingWithError`.

On iOS/macOS, every stream that isn't a QuickTime file (for example MP3, WAV or M4A audio) is labelled "public.mpeg-4", so those formats may fail to play from a stream on Apple platforms. Windows uses the shared StreamExtensions detector, which handles these formats. GetStreamContentType only checks for the `ftyp` box and returns `com.apple.quicktime-movie` for brand "qt". Every other path returns `StreamAssetResourceLoader.DefaultContentType` or the literal "public.mpeg-4". StreamExtensions.GetMimeType, which knows many more formats, is not used here.

When one StreamMediaSource replaces another, the previous StreamDataSourceFactory Java peer is disposed while the player's current ProgressiveMediaSource still references it. Until SetMediaSource is called, the loader thread may call into the disposed peer and fail. CreateMediaItemFromStream calls `currentStreamDataSourceFactory?.Dispose(); currentStreamDataSourceFactory = null;` during SetPlayerData, which awaits artwork download. `Player.SetMediaSource(...)` is only called later in PlatformUpdateSource (line 399). StreamDataSourceFactory is a sealed Java.Lang.Object with no (IntPtr, JniHandleOwnership) activation constructor.

The sample page crashes the app when the network fetch fails, because the exception escapes an async void lifecycle override. `protected override async void OnAppearing()` calls `await using var networkStream = await httpClient.GetStreamAsync(StreamingUrls.BuckBunny);` outside any try/catch. Only the later UpdateSourceStream call has a catch. An HttpRequestException (offline, DNS failure) is unobserved in an async void method and terminates the app.

The sample disposes the MemoryStream the MediaElement is still playing from, both before the replacement is copied and in OnDisappearing. The semaphore doesn't serialise anything, so the player may read a disposed stream and the source can be swapped while the page is going away. UpdateSourceStream calls `await ReleaseSourceStream()` first, then `sourceStream = new MemoryStream(); await stream.CopyToAsync(sourceStream);`. The new stream is assigned outside the semaphore, and `MediaElement.Source` still points at the disposed stream until the copy finishes. ReleaseSourceStream checks `if (sourceStream is null) return;` before `WaitAsync`. OnDisappearing (line 44) disposes the stream without clearing MediaElement.Source.

The change edits an existing baseline test, which is part of the locked acceptance set, in a way unrelated to the stream-source story. The diff replaces `await Task.Delay(100, TestContext.Current.CancellationToken);` with a `while (!cts.Token.IsCancellationRequested) { await Task.Delay(1, ...); }` loop in LoadViewAsync_CancellationTokenExpired. acceptance.md says the baseline's tests are the locked acceptance tests.

The diff edits the agent's own coding-style instructions file, adding a new rule and removing the file's final code fence. This change to the agent's instructions wasn't requested and needs separate human review. It adds an "## Argument Validation:" section that prescribes ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull. The final hunk replaces the trailing "```" line with an empty line.

The diff includes changes outside the story's scope: a behaviour change to artwork file loading, the static HttpClient becoming per-instance, member reordering in three MediaSource classes, a reformat of all the listener stubs, and whitespace in PopupsPage. These make the diff harder to review. `stream = File.Open(normalizedFilePath, FileMode.Create)` becomes `File.OpenRead(...)` (the old code truncated the artwork file). `static readonly HttpClient client` becomes an instance field. The Path and implicit operators are moved in File/Resource/UriMediaSource. Each one-line `public void OnX(...) { }` stub is expanded to multiple lines.

The Apple manager adds its own magic-byte sniffer next to the new shared StreamExtensions.GetMimeType, so there are two sniffers that already give different answers. `static string GetStreamContentType(Stream stream)` re-implements the ftyp check with its own seek/restore logic. StreamExtensions.shared.cs has `internal static string GetMimeType(this Stream stream)` with the same check.

The MIME sniffer classifies any stream whose first byte is 0x47 ('G') as MPEG-TS, so unknown content can be labelled video/mp2t instead of the default. The class summary also wrongly says it is Windows-only. `if (header.Length >= 1 && header[0] is 0x47) return "video/mp2t";` checks one byte and doesn't look for the sync byte repeating at 188-byte intervals. The doc comment says "Extension methods for <see cref="Stream"/> on Windows platform." on a .shared.cs file.

The typed HttpClient registration for the page may have no effect, so the page may get a default HttpClient without the resilience handler. The existing pattern in this file registers the typed client on a view model, not on a page. `builder.Services.AddHttpClient<MediaElementFromStreamPage>().AddStandardResilienceHandler(...)` registers the page as a typed client. `services.AddTransientWithShellRoute<MediaElementFromStreamPage, MediaElementFromStreamViewModel>()` registers the page again afterwards, and the later registration wins. The constructor takes `HttpClient` directly. The existing example registers `AddHttpClient<ByteArrayToImageSourceConverterViewModel>()`.

The new StreamMediaSource test only checks the returned type. Nothing tests that the Stream is stored, the implicit operators, ToString, the MediaSourceConverter branch, or the platform data-source code, so a FromStream that ignored its argument would still pass. MediaSourceFromStreamShouldBeStreamMediaSource asserts only `mediaSource.Should().BeAssignableTo<StreamMediaSource>()`. No test covers StreamDataSourceFactory, StreamAssetResourceLoader or `StreamMediaSource streamMediaSource => streamMediaSource.ToString()` in the converter.

On Tizen, setting a StreamMediaSource throws NotSupportedException from inside the source-update path instead of logging or failing the media, which may surface as an unhandled exception from a property change. `throw new NotSupportedException($"{nameof(StreamMediaSource)} is not yet supported on Tizen...")` inside PlatformUpdateSource. Other unsupported cases in the managers log a warning (for example `Logger.LogWarning("Invalid file path for ResourceMediaSource.")` on macios).

After the move, the scripts' fallback repo root (used when AO_REPO_ROOT is unset) points at `packages/cli/src/assets` or `dist/assets` instead of the repository root, so running a script directly gives wrong results: ao-update.sh does a partial update and then fails. Both scripts still compute `REPO_ROOT="${AO_REPO_ROOT:-$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)}"` (ao-update.sh:43, ao-doctor.sh:31). That was correct at `scripts/` but is now one directory below `assets/`. When ao-update.sh runs directly, it `cd`s into that directory, passes the `git rev-parse` check (it is still inside the work tree), runs `git pull --ff-only`, `pnpm install` and the filtered builds, and then exits at `cd "$REPO_ROOT/packages/ao"`. When ao-doctor.sh runs directly, it picks source-checkout layout and FAILs every node_modules, core-build and launcher check. Only the CLI path, which now always exports AO_REPO_ROOT from runRepoScript, is correct.

When a git source checkout lacks the bundled update script, `ao update` quietly switches to the npm-global flow instead of failing with a rebuild hint, so the checkout is never updated and the user may be offered a global npm install that shadows their source launcher. handleGitUpdate does `if (!hasRepoScript("ao-update.sh")) { ... await handleNpmUpdate(opts, "npm-global"); return; }`. hasRepoScript only checks `<CLI_DIST_ROOT>/assets/scripts`, so a checkout whose dist was built without the `cp -r src/assets dist/` step reaches this branch. handleNpmUpdate then compares against the npm registry. If a source checkout on main is not behind the published version, it prints "Already on latest version" and returns without running git pull or a rebuild. Otherwise it prompts to run `npm install -g @aoagents/ao@latest` (hard-coded npm, even for pnpm users). It also prints "--skip-smoke and --smoke-only only apply to git source installs. Ignoring." to a user who is on a git source install. No spec line or test shows this fallback was asked for; the new test only mocks hasRepoScript to false.

The update script now runs from `packages/cli/dist/assets/scripts/`, which the script itself deletes (`clean`) and recreates (`build`) partway through. It keeps working only because bash holds the unlinked inode open, which is fragile if the build ever overwrites files in place. runRepoScript resolves the script under CLI_DIST_ROOT (`dist/assets/scripts/ao-update.sh` for a built checkout). The script then runs `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-cli clean` (package.json: `rm -rf dist`) and `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-cli build` (`tsc && cp -r src/assets dist/`) while bash is still reading that same file.

The change deletes two existing negative tests for git-install detection and rewrites a third, which weakens the locked baseline coverage for classifyInstallPath to a single all-false case. The diff removes "returns 'unknown' when .git exists but scripts/ao-update.sh does not" and "returns 'unknown' when scripts/ao-update.sh exists but .git does not", and renames the neither-exists case. classifyInstallPath now returns "git" on `existsSync(resolve(repoRoot, ".git"))` alone. Acceptance.md says the baseline's tests are the locked acceptance tests.

The packaged-install doctor test forces `AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT=package-install`, so the shell's own layout auto-detection is never exercised and a wrong detection rule would pass. The test env sets `AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT: "package-install"`, which skips the `if [ -z "$SCRIPT_LAYOUT" ]` branch in ao-doctor.sh:33-39 (`package.json` && `dist/index.js` && no `packages` dir). No test runs the script without the override against a package-shaped directory.

Documentation still lists the update and doctor scripts at their old `scripts/` paths, which no longer exist. docs/design-onboarding-improvements.html lines 693, 694 and 1182 list `scripts/ao-update.sh` and `scripts/ao-doctor.sh`. The diff renames both to `packages/cli/src/assets/scripts/`.

trackUpdate now writes partition_meta right away even when the manager has not loaded from storage. If the Durable Object wakes from hibernation, the first client update overwrites the stored meta with only the current quarter, and earlier partitions can no longer be reached. BoardRoom uses this.ctx.acceptWebSocket (the hibernation API), and loading happens only in fetch() (board-room.ts:36-37: loadUpdates/loadFromStorage). webSocketMessage → trackUpdate never loads. On a freshly woken instance partitionMeta is null, so lines 112-118 build {partitions:[partName]...}, set metaChanged=true and call `void savePartitionMeta()`, which puts that over the persisted 'partition_meta'. The old trackUpdate only scheduled the partition-updates save and never wrote meta. Nothing calls loadFromStorage before this write, and there is no blockConcurrencyWhile in the constructor.

applyClientUpdate returns true without checking anything when no Y.Doc exists, which is the normal state of a websocket-only session. Corrupt client updates are therefore still buffered, broadcast, persisted and replayed to new clients, so the new rejection branch in board-room only works when a doc happens to be loaded. `if (doc) { try { Y.applyUpdate(doc, payload) } catch { return false } } return true;` Only getOrCreateDoc creates doc, and only the AI, thumbnail and snapshot paths call it. destroyDoc nulls it again when the last socket closes. board-room.ts:118-125 then calls pushUpdate, trackUpdate, broadcast and scheduleSave on the payload.

Rotation may only be half-wired. Shapes now render rotated and point hit tests unrotate, but marquee selection still tests the unrotated getBounds box. A rotated shape's visible area and the area that selects it can therefore disagree. findShapesInRect uses `def.getBounds(data)`, and the plugin getBounds functions (e.g. plugins/usketch-plugin-shape-basic/src/shared/bounds.ts) ignore rotation. Meanwhile shape-layer.tsx applies `transform: rotate(${rotation}deg)`, and the hitTest functions are wrapped in withRotation. Only the store's spatial index (board-store.ts shapeToBounds) uses getRotatedAABB.

The change rewrites server sync and persistence code (update validation order, load memoisation, save debouncing, partition-meta persistence, thumbnail style parsing), but the change's own tests and exports are about shape rotation. These server hunks have no test, and one of them adds the data-loss path above. diff.patch changes apps/server/src/board-room.ts, rooms/yjs-sync.ts, rooms/partition-manager.ts and rooms/thumbnail-handler.ts. The only test added is packages/shared/src/__tests__/rotation.test.ts, and it covers rotation utilities only. No server test exercises the new applyClientUpdate return value, loadPromise or saveScheduled logic.

normalizeAngle, snapAngle and deltaToLocal are exported as public API, but no production code uses them. They are dead code that the tests exercise only on their own. A grep for deltaToLocal|snapAngle|normalizeAngle matches only rotation.ts, index.ts, rotation.test.ts and a v1 design doc. No plugin or engine imports them, and no rotate tool or handle calls them.

The GPU path forwards the raw rotation without safeRotation, and the rect shader may not apply rotation at all. GPU-rendered rects can therefore disagree with the DOM rendering and the hit testing this change makes rotation-aware. `data[off + 15] = r.rotation ?? 0;` passes NaN or Infinity through. rect.wgsl names rotation only in the params comment (line 15), and grep finds no cos or sin use in the shader.

The shared package's reference docs do not cover the eight newly exported rotation helpers (safeRotation, withRotation, getRotatedAABB, etc.), or that plugin hitTest functions must now be wrapped to support rotation. packages/shared/src/index.ts adds the rotation exports. The only rotation text in shared.mdx is `rotation?: number;` at line 48.

vTaskSwitchContext now refuses every context switch while the running task has preemption disabled, including when that task blocks, delays, suspends or deletes itself. The task keeps running even though the kernel has moved it to a delayed, event, suspended or termination list. The new guard `if( pxCurrentTCBs[ xCoreID ]->xPreemptionDisable != pdFALSE ) { xYieldPendings[ xCoreID ] = pdTRUE; } else if( uxSchedulerSuspended ...` returns without switching. It does not check whether the current task is still Ready. Trigger: after vTaskPreemptionDisable(NULL), the task calls vTaskDelay(10). vTaskDelay (tasks.c:2491) calls prvAddCurrentTaskToDelayedList and then taskYIELD_WITHIN_API (tasks.c:2504). That reaches vTaskSwitchContext, which only latches the flag, so the 'delayed' task keeps executing. vTaskDelete(NULL) has the same problem: tasks.c:2320 yields after the TCB is queued for the idle task to free, so the idle task can free the stack of a task that is still running. The same applies to vTaskDelete or vTaskSuspend on another core's task: prvYieldCore at tasks.c:2324 IPIs that core, and its vTaskSwitchContext also refuses to switch. Nothing else in tasks.c stops a preemption-disabled task from blocking: xPreemptionDisable is only read at lines 945, 1251, 2894, 4897, 4950 and 5234.

xTaskRemoveFromEventList, xTaskResumeFromISR and the two notify-from-ISR paths now report 'no higher-priority task woken' whenever this core already had a yield pending. A caller that uses a separate woken flag per call, or that relies on the return value, can skip a required portYIELD_FROM_ISR even though a higher-priority task was unblocked. Each site now requires `( xYieldPendingBefore == pdFALSE ) && ( xYieldPendings[ portGET_CORE_ID() ] != pdFALSE )` before returning pdTRUE or setting *pxHigherPriorityTaskWoken (tasks.c:3531, 5504, 8218, and the matching block near 8351). Example: an ISR calls xSemaphoreGiveFromISR(a,&w1) and then xSemaphoreGiveFromISR(b,&w2). The first call sets xYieldPendings[core]. The second returns pdFALSE even though it unblocked a higher-priority task, which breaks the documented meaning of the woken flag. The single-core branches (e.g. tasks.c:5478) still report it based on priority.

An explicit taskYIELD() from a preemption-disabled task is now silently turned into a latched pending flag. This changes cooperative-yield behaviour the API docs never described, and the latched flag stops prvYieldForTask from considering this core until the task re-enables preemption. vTaskSwitchContext sets `xYieldPendings[ xCoreID ] = pdTRUE` and returns. prvYieldForTask (tasks.c:932) skips any core where `xYieldPendings[ xCoreID ] == pdFALSE` is not true. The vTaskPreemptionDisable docs in include/task.h:1425-1453 only say the task 'will not be preempted'. They say nothing about voluntary yields being suppressed.

The change alters SMP scheduling semantics in five places but adds no tests. Nothing shows that the time-slice, the yield-return or the vTaskSwitchContext changes behave as intended, or that blocking with preemption disabled still works. diff.patch touches only tasks.c, and the export contains no unit-test sources (the only *test* path is portable/Paradigm/Tern_EE/large_untested/port.c). acceptance.md points to story.md and tests.lock, but neither is in the packet or the export, so no locked test can be checked against these code paths.

The same snapshot, yield and compare block is copied into four call sites instead of being folded into prvYieldForTask or a helper. Future fixes to the yield-reporting rule may land in only some of them. The identical `BaseType_t xYieldPendingBefore = xYieldPendings[ portGET_CORE_ID() ]; prvYieldForTask( ... ); if( ( xYieldPendingBefore == pdFALSE ) && ...` pattern appears at tasks.c:3527, 5500, 8214 and about 8351. Two of the copies compare with `== pdTRUE` and two with `!= pdFALSE`.

The ENTROPY expression calls `.otherwise()` on the result of `F.sum(...)` rather than on a `F.when(...)`, so every generated script with an ENTROPY metric fails at runtime when the expression is built. `_distributional_agg_expr` returns `F.sum(F.when({cv} > 0, -{p} * F.log({p}))).otherwise(F.lit(0.0))`. The `.otherwise` is attached to the Column that `F.sum` returns. Spark's `Column.otherwise` raises IllegalArgumentException ("otherwise() can only be applied on a Column previously generated by when() function") on any other Column. The default test fixture `_pipeline_full` uses `DistributionalMetric.ENTROPY`, so the full script breaks inside `build_layer2b`. The tests only run `ast.parse`, so they pass.

MODE returns an arbitrary category (whichever row `F.first` meets first) instead of the category with the largest share, so the MODE feature column holds wrong values. `if metric == DistributionalMetric.MODE: return f'F.first(F.col("{cat_col}"), ignorenulls=True).alias(...)'`. It runs inside `_shares_{i}.groupBy(id, time).agg(...)` with no ordering by `{cat}_..._cat_val`. `first()` inside a groupBy aggregate is non-deterministic and ignores the share column entirely. Any distributional categorical configured with MODE (see `_pipeline_all_metrics`) produces this column.

Categorical values and field names are pasted into generated Python source without escaping. A value containing a double quote breaks the script, and a crafted value (for example one returned by a `domain_resolver` that reads distinct values from the facts table) can inject arbitrary Python into the script the user then runs on the cluster. `build_layer2a` builds `f'(F.col("{cat_field.name}") == "{cat_val}")'` and `f'...alias("{alias}")'` with plain f-string interpolation. `PivotedColumn.__init__` only checks values for the `__` separator (`_check_name_part`). docs/general_plan.md (Plan 09) says domain values may come from `SELECT DISTINCT` on the data. A value like `A"), __import__("os").system("..."), F.lit("` still parses as valid Python and would run. The same unescaped `f'"{c}"'` pattern is used for id, time and measurement names in every build_* method. Only table names use `!r`.

The Plan 16 criterion "All transformations are lazy until the returned callable is invoked" is not met. The generator returns a plain script string with no callable, and each step runs an eager `saveAsTable` action, while the class docstring says everything is lazy. docs/general_plan.md Plan 16 says the final output is "a `PySparkOutput` containing a callable that, when invoked with a `SparkSession`, executes the full pipeline", and its acceptance criterion requires laziness until that call. Every build_* method instead emits `...write.mode('overwrite').saveAsTable(...)` (lines 78, 127, 211, 286, 388). That is a Spark action that runs immediately and overwrites tables. `generate` returns `PySparkOutput(code=full_code)`, a string. The docstring at line 36 says "All generated transformations are lazy". The script also uses an undefined global `spark` instead of taking a session as a parameter.

Several distinct temporal operators are emitted with identical expressions. PROM_P is the same as PROM_U, SUM_P the same as SUM_U, XM the same as FREQ, and RATIO is just a windowed SUM. The feature table may therefore contain duplicate columns under names that suggest different features, and nobody has signed off what these operators mean. `_temporal_pyspark_expr`: the PROM_P branch returns the same `F.avg(...).over(frame_w)` as PROM_U. SUM_P matches SUM_U. The XM branch is a copy of FREQ. RATIO returns `F.sum({col_ref}).over({frame_w})`, which is not a ratio. No spec or code in the repo defines these operators differently, so the builder's reading is an unrecorded assumption.

When there are no Layer 3 features (or no Layer 2A columns), the generated code is a syntax error, because the template always adds a trailing comma line after the list it joins. `build_layer3` emits `'    "mob",
' + f"{feat_list},
" + ")"`. With `pipeline.layer3` empty, `feat_list` is `""`, so the output contains a line holding only `,`, which is invalid Python. `build_layer2a` has the same issue with `f"{agg_list},
"` (line 125). `build_final_join` does guard on `pipeline.layer3`, but `build_layer3` does not. An empty layer3 can happen through `operators_override`.

The tests check only that the generated text parses and contains certain keywords. They never run the code against a Spark or mocked session and never check computed values, so they cannot catch the broken ENTROPY expression or the wrong MODE logic. Every assertion is `_is_valid_python(...)` (ast.parse) or a substring check such as `"crossJoin" in self._code()` or `"features" in code`. `test_empty_layer2b_returns_comment` (line 278) asserts `"layer2b" not in out.code or "no distributional" in out.code`, which accepts almost any output. Plan 16 allows a mocked SparkSession, but none is used.

The `generate()` override weakens the public interface. It declares return type `object` instead of `FeatureStoreOutput`, and its type checks use `assert`, which is stripped under `python -O`. `def generate(self, pipeline: FeatureStorePipeline) -> object:` followed by `assert isinstance(result, FeatureStoreOutput)` and `assert isinstance(result.code, _PS)`. It also re-imports `PySparkOutput` as `_PS` even though the module already imports it at the top.

The change contains dead or misleading code: a conditional whose two branches are identical, an unused helper, and an unused import in the generated header. `col_ref = (f'F.col("{src_col}")' if not isinstance(feat.source, DistributionalColumn) else f'F.col("{src_col}")')` has the same value on both branches. `_spark_read` (line 51) is never called. `_HEADER` imports `SparkSession`, but the generated script never uses it and relies on a global `spark`.

The registration check in checkin is never awaited, so it never blocks: staff can check in a participant who is not registered for the event. `if (!this.eventService.isRegistered(user!, event))`: EventService.isRegistered is `async` (event_service.ts:5), so it returns a Promise, which is always truthy, and `!promise` is always false. Trigger: POST /events/<slug>/check-in with the eventID of an event the participant never registered for. The 'não registado' branch is skipped and `checkin` attaches a row to event_checkins.

The dialog calls hooks after a conditional early return, so opening the scanner changes the hook count between renders and React throws, which breaks the check-in UI. `if (!isOpen) { return null; }` comes before `const tuyau = useTuyau();` and `useForm(...)`. page.tsx:386-391 mounts the dialog for staff with `isOpen={scannerModalOpen}` (initially false). Clicking the QrCode sets it true, the same component instance renders two more hooks than before, and React raises 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render'.

The staff QR check-in button only renders inside the `!isRegistered` block, so a staff member who is registered for the event can't open the scanner. The `<QrCode onClick={() => setScannerModalOpen(true)} />` is nested inside `{!isRegistered && ( <div ...> ... )}` (lines 290-317). No other control sets scannerModalOpen.

If a participant profile has no linked user, the handler goes on with a null user and crashes with a 500 instead of returning the 'not found' message. `const user = await User.findBy("participantProfileId", profile?.id);` can return null, and nothing checks it. The code then calls `isCheckedIn(user!, event)`, which reads `user.id` in `.where("user_id", user.id)` and throws a TypeError.

The scanner fires continuously while a code is in view, so one badge sends many concurrent check-in POSTs. These race past the isCheckedIn check, hit the unique constraint as a 500, and show 'já checked-in' error toasts for a check-in that just succeeded. The scanner keeps `allowMultiple={true}` and `scanDelay={0}`, and each `onScan` calls `handleCheckIN` → `post(...)`. On the server, `isCheckedIn` then `checkin` is a check-then-insert with no transaction or conflict handling, against `table.unique(["event_id", "user_id"])` in the new migration.

The new seeder creates a staff account with the known credential staff@eneiconf.pt / 'password' and has no dev-only guard, so seeding a non-dev database creates a staff login anyone can guess. `User.create({ email: "staff@eneiconf.pt", ... })` and `accounts.create({ id: "credentials:staff@eneiconf.pt", password: "password" })`, with no `app.inDev` check (compare 2_account_seeder.dev.ts:11). It also inserts `Department.create({ id: 99, ... })` with a fixed id, so a second run fails on the primary key.

A mock seeder with no environment guard gives a staff profile to whatever user has id 1, which grants staff check-in and product-collect powers in any environment where seeders run. `const user = await User.findOrFail(1); ... await user.related("staffProfile").associate(staffProfile);`. Unlike 2_account_seeder.dev.ts, which returns early when `!app.inDev`, this file has no such check, and its name doesn't follow the numbered ordering.

The new check-in endpoint has no tests: authorisation, unregistered participant, duplicate check-in and unknown slug are all unchecked, and the unawaited isRegistered bug above went through because of it. diff.patch adds no test files. The behaviour is in EventsController.checkin, EventService.isCheckedIn/checkin and the new route `actions:events.checkin`.

Moving the staff check to the top of `role` changes the role of every user who is both staff and a participant or promoter, so promoter-only UI (common/page.tsx shows only for role 'promoter') disappears for staff-promoters. The story asked for check-in, not a role change. `if (this.isStaff()) return "staff" as const;` now comes before the participant and promoter checks. config/inertia.ts:31 sends `role: user.role` to the client, and inertia/components/common/page.tsx:13 returns null unless the role is 'promoter'.

`show` now loads staffProfile on every event page view but never uses it: an extra query on a public page. `await user?.load("staffProfile");` was added, but `isStaff()` now reads `this.staffProfileId` (user.ts:110) and the render props never include staffProfile.

The staff guard's denial behaviour changed for every route that uses it (including product collect) from redirecting to signup to redirecting back with a flash, which is outside the story's scope. `return ctx.response.redirect().toRoute("pages:signup")` was replaced by `ctx.session.flashErrors({ message: "Unauthorized" }); return ctx.response.redirect().back();`. routes.ts:171 also applies middleware.staff() to the product collect route.

The check-in table's foreign keys are nullable and have no onDelete rule, so deleting a user or event that has check-ins will fail. Rolling back drops every recorded check-in with no export. `table.integer("event_id").references("id").inTable("events");` and the same for user_id, with no `.notNullable()` or `.onDelete(...)`. `down()` is `this.schema.dropTable(this.tableName)`. The guard is keyed on whoever triggered the run, not on the PR's author. If a human pushes to, rebases or re-runs a Dependabot PR, the job is skipped, and GitHub treats a skipped job as passing for required checks, so the PR can merge without the regression gate. `if: github.actor == 'dependabot[bot]'`. `github.actor` is the user who triggered this event, so after a maintainer pushes a commit or re-runs the job it no longer equals `dependabot[bot]`. `github.event.pull_request.user.login` would identify the PR's author instead.

The regression gate compares only High and Critical totals, so a PR that removes one High CVE and adds a different one passes. `critical_regression = pr_counts.get("Critical", 0) > base_counts.get("Critical", 0)` and the same for High compare counts from `counts()` and ignore vulnerability IDs. A new High match is hidden whenever another High match disappears. The `underfixed_updates` check only covers packages that still have a fixed High/Critical version in the PR image, so it doesn't catch this.

The `run_id` dispatch input is pasted straight into the shell script, so whoever dispatches the workflow can inject commands into a job that holds an issues:write token. A value containing `"` or `$(...)` breaks out of the string, and a value with a newline can also inject extra outputs. The gate runs whatever `anchore/grype` tag is newest when it runs, found through an unauthenticated API call, with no digest pin. The CoreSync sync server still accepts unauthenticated requests even with Auth:UseEntraId=true, so the 'CoreSync auth' change doesn't actually protect the sync channel: anyone who can reach the Web server can pull or push sync data without a token. With real Entra ID tokens, TenantId may come out null and UserId may be the token's 'sub' instead of 'oid'. The middleware reads FindFirstValue("tid") ?? FindFirstValue("tenant_id") and FindFirstValue("oid") ?? FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier). AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApi in Program.cs:34-35 doesn't turn off MapInboundClaims. When mapping is on, 'oid' becomes http://schemas.microsoft.com/identity/claims/objectidentifier and 'sub' becomes NameIdentifier, and Entra tokens carry no 'tenant_id'. The tests can't catch this: TestJwtGenerator adds both 'tid' and 'tenant_id', and both 'oid' and NameIdentifier with the same value, so API_ExtractsTenantContext passes whichever claim the middleware actually reads.

They pass against a generic JwtBearer scheme added on top of the DevAuthHandler registration, so the Entra configuration (issuer, audience, AzureAd section) is untested. The factory then calls services.AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme).AddJwtBearer(...) with TestJwtGenerator's symmetric key and issuer, and switches the default schemes over to it. The Microsoft.Identity.Web branch in Program.cs:32-48 is never built.

NativeAOT builds that use the trimmable typemap now fail with MSB4057, because `_AndroidRunNativeCompile` depends on a target that is only defined in the LlvmIr typemap file, and that file is not imported for the trimmable typemap. NativeAOT.targets:270 has `DependsOnTargets="_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesignerUpdateItems;NativeCompile"`. NativeAOT.targets is always imported for NativeAOT (Microsoft.Android.Sdk.targets:36, `Microsoft.Android.Sdk.$(_AndroidRuntime).targets`). `_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesignerUpdateItems` is defined only in Microsoft.Android.Sdk.TypeMap.LlvmIr.targets, which Xamarin.Android.Common.targets:2880-2881 imports only when `'$(_AndroidTypeMapImplementation)' != 'trimmable'`. The trimmable+NativeAOT combination is supported: Microsoft.Android.Sdk.TypeMap.Trimmable.targets:9 imports Trimmable.NativeAOT.targets for `_AndroidRuntime == NativeAOT`. MSBuild fails when a DependsOnTargets entry names a target that does not exist, unlike AfterTargets. A Condition-guarded call, or defining the target outside the LlvmIr file, would avoid this.

The swap uses any file that happens to be in `obj/.../prelink/` and nothing ever deletes old copies, so after a library upgrade the app can silently ship an old rewritten copy of that library in place of the current one. `_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesignerUpdateItems` swaps every ResolvedFileToPublish .dll for which `Exists('$(IntermediateOutputPath)prelink/%(Filename)%(Extension)')` is true. It does not use the task's `ModifiedAssemblies` output. PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesigner.RunTask only calls `Directory.CreateDirectory (OutputDirectory)` and writes a file when `ProcessAssemblyDesigner` returns true; it never removes old files. Trigger: publish with library A v1, which has a legacy Resource designer, so prelink/A.dll is written. Upgrade A to v2, which uses the designer assembly or has no legacy designer. The task reruns (or is skipped), `FindResourceDesigner` returns false so nothing is written, and the old prelink/A.dll still exists. The Exists() swap then replaces v2 with the rewritten v1 before ILLink.

The up-to-date check only looks at a stamp file, not the files it produces, so a deleted or missing prelink copy may never be regenerated, and an unrewritten legacy-designer library then goes to ILLink, which no longer keeps the designer root. `_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesigner` has `Outputs="$(_AndroidStampDirectory)_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesigner.stamp"`, and its `<FileWrites Include="@(_PreTrimmingModifiedAssembly)" />` is added only when the target actually runs. If prelink/*.dll is removed (manual clean of obj/prelink, or possibly IncrementalClean on a build where the target was skipped and FileWrites lacked them), the stamp is still newer than the inputs, the task is skipped, Exists() is false, and the original library passes to ILLink. The old post-trim rewrite (removed from PostTrimmingPipeline.cs) and the TrimmerRootDescriptor (removed from Resource.Designer.targets) no longer back this up. Before this change the rewrite ran on every build because `_PostTrimmingPipeline` has no Inputs/Outputs. The same stamp check also skips the task when a newly added input .dll has an older timestamp than the stamp.

The guard checks the branch of the session sending the shutdown, not the branch of the implementer it targets. In the documented team-lead workflow the guard therefore never blocks, or it judges the wrong branch. Lines 126-129 run `git symbolic-ref --short HEAD` in process.cwd(), which is the lead's checkout. Line 135 then allows the shutdown when that branch is `main` or `master`. templates/skills/dev-team-task/SKILL.md:154 has Drucker spawn one implementer per issue, each on its own branch `feat/<issue>-<description>` and named `{agent}-implement-...`. Trigger: Drucker is on `main` and sends `{to:"voss-implement-773", message:{type:"shutdown_request"}}` while feat/773 has no reviews. Line 135 exits 0 and the shutdown goes through. If Drucker is on a reviewed feat/A, shutting down the implementer of an unreviewed feat/B is also allowed. Nothing maps `tool_input.to` to that agent's branch.

Real review sidecars never count as evidence, because the guard only looks for the branch name inside the sidecar's filename. Once review is done, the guard keeps blocking every implementer shutdown unless --force-shutdown is used. Line 147 is `files.some((f) => f.includes(sanitizedBranch) && f.endsWith(".json"))`. ADR-029 (docs/adr/029-stateless-commit-gates.md:48) and review-gate.js:199 name sidecars `<agent>--<contentHash>.json`, with no branch in the name. merge-gate.js:153-156 handles this by checking the sidecar's `branch` JSON field first and using the filename only as a fallback. The new guard never reads the file contents.

Any sidecar for the branch is enough to allow shutdown, so an implementer can still be shut down before findings are routed and acknowledged. That is the rule the hook and README say it enforces. Lines 152-155 allow shutdown as soon as one matching .json file exists. The guard does not check for unresolved `[DEFECT]` findings or acknowledgement, and does not exclude `.cleanup-manifest.json` or symlinks. merge-gate.js:130-147 excludes both. dev-team-task/SKILL.md:80 says 'Implementing agents must remain alive until all findings have been routed and acknowledged'. The README row added at line 153 says 'before review findings are routed'.

The test for the 'review evidence present' case uses a sidecar filename that the review tooling never writes. It passes, but it hides the fact that real sidecars are never recognised, and no test covers the lead running on main. The test writes `knuth--feat-123-test.json`, but sidecars are actually named `<agent>--<contentHash>.json` (ADR-029). It also writes a `branch` field into the JSON that the hook never reads. Every test runs with cwd on `feat/123-test`. None runs with the sender on `main`, and none targets an implementer on a different branch from the sender.

A plain-text message to an implementer that merely mentions the word shutdown_request is treated as a shutdown and may be blocked. Also, the bypass flag is matched anywhere in text the model writes. Line 90 is `typeof message === "string" && message.includes("shutdown_request")`, so a status note like 'do not send shutdown_request yet' is treated as a shutdown. Line 97 is `/--force-shutdown/i.test(messageStr)` on the same model-authored text, so the lead agent can bypass the guard by adding the flag. The only record is a console.warn.

The header comment describes behaviour the hook does not have. The comment says the hook 'blocks premature shutdown of implementing agents that have open, unreviewed PRs'. The code never looks up PRs; it only checks the local branch and sidecar filenames (lines 124-150).

The guard copies merge-gate's sanitisation and sidecar lookup instead of sharing them, and the copy has already drifted from merge-gate's stricter matching. Line 142 repeats `branch.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9-]/g, "-")` from merge-gate.js:63. The guard also leaves out the `branch`-field match, the symlink filter and the manifest exclusion that merge-gate.js:128-160 has. The hooks directory already has a `lib/` folder for shared code.

The generated probe for non-wrapper binaries looks up a name with literal double quotes around it (e.g. `"jq"`). `command -v` then finds nothing, so Check 3 fails on the first system binary (jq) for every GCE verification run, and the sandbox-image check fails the same way. The heredoc delimiter `<<SH` is unquoted. In an unquoted heredoc a backslash before `"` is kept, so line 279 renders as `binary_path="$(command -v \"jq\" || true)"`. Inside `$(...)` the remote `sh -c` parses `\"jq\"` as an escaped quote, so the argument becomes the literal string `"jq"`. `command -v` returns empty, and the script prints `missing_binary:jq` and exits 1. That makes `gce_ssh` fail at line 296 and `fail "Failed to validate runtime binary jq ..."` fire. jq is the first entry in scripts/docker/runtime-binaries.json and has no wrapper, so every run takes this path. The baseline used `command -v "${binary}"` inside a quoted `<<'SH'` heredoc, where this problem could not occur.

The binary list now comes from the CI checkout, not from the image being verified. If the checked-out ref differs from the deployed app image or the separately built sandbox image, the gate checks the wrong set of binaries: it can fail on binaries the image never promised, or pass while missing ones the image's manifest lists. `entries_json="$(jq ... "${runtime_binary_manifest_in_repo}")"` reads `${repo_root}/scripts/docker/runtime-binaries.json`. The in-image manifest (`/usr/local/share/openclaw/runtime-binaries.json`) is now only checked with `test -f` at lines 240-243 and its contents are ignored. In .github/workflows/verify.yml, `actions/checkout@v4` checks out the workflow ref, not `inputs.deployed_ref`. The baseline probe queried the manifest inside the target with `jq ... "${manifest_path}"`.

The wrapper directory is now taken from the CI runner's environment, not the target's. The wrapper path checked can differ from where the image actually installed its wrappers. Line 358 sets `runtime_wrapper_bin="${OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN:-/opt/daisy/bin}"` on the runner. The Dockerfile and Dockerfile.sandbox set `ENV OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN=/opt/daisy/bin` inside the images, and the baseline probe read that variable inside the container. Now the default is hard-coded on the runner side and can drift from the image's value.

The validation attributes on SendMailRequest are never enforced, so a missing `to` or `subject` field gives an unhandled 500 instead of a 400, and the Body size limit, the ContentType allowlist and the Subject length limit are not applied. The minimal-API handler binds `SendMailRequest request`, and the repo registers no validation filter: grep finds no AddValidation, IEndpointFilter or Validator call in src. So `[Required, MinLength(1)] To`, `[MaxLength(1_048_576)] Body` and `[RegularExpression("^(html|plain)$")] ContentType` are decorative. A JSON body without `to` makes `request.To.Length` throw NullReferenceException at line 32. A null `subject` reaches `message.Subject = request.Subject` in MailSendingService.BuildMimeMessage (line 56), which may throw ArgumentNullException. Any ContentType other than "html" silently becomes plain text. The empty-To case also returns the misleading `InvalidEmailAddress` message.

Only InvalidOperationException is caught, and it is mapped to 404 'MailboxNotFound'. SMTP failures (auth, connect, rejected recipients) therefore come back as unhandled 500s. MailKit state errors that may derive from InvalidOperationException would be misreported as 'mailbox not found'. The SendMailFailed message added for this case is never used. `catch (InvalidOperationException) { return Results.NotFound(new { message = localizer["MailboxNotFound"].Value }); }` is the only handler around `mailSendingService.SendMailAsync`. MailSendingService.SendViaSmtpAsync calls ConnectAsync, AuthenticateAsync and SendAsync, plus `protector.Unprotect` (which throws CryptographicException), all with no try/catch. The new `SendMailFailed` key in ApiMessages*.resx is not referenced anywhere. By contrast, MailTestEndpoints catches SocketException, IOException, SslHandshakeException and AuthenticationException explicitly.

The double-send guard is checked before an async JS call but only set after it, so a quick double-click on Send can deliver the same email twice. SendAsync runs `if (_isSending) return;` and then `await GetBodyAndContentTypeAsync()`, which makes JS interop calls (`quillInterop.isEmpty` and `getHtml`). `_isSending = true;` is only set after validation (line 290). A second click handled during those awaits sees `_isSending == false`, and the button is not disabled yet, so both invocations POST /api/mail/send.

Every send writes the user's mailbox address and all To recipients' email addresses (personal data) to the logs at Information level. `logger.LogInformation("Mail sent from {From} to {To} via mailbox {MailboxId}", mailbox.EmailAddress, string.Join(", ", request.To), mailbox.Id);` The other log lines in this service log only the MailboxId.

On IMAP servers without SPECIAL-USE/XLIST, `GetFolder(SpecialFolder.Sent)` may throw instead of returning null. The fallback lookup by name is then never reached, and the sent message is silently left out of the Sent folder. `var sent = client.GetFolder(SpecialFolder.Sent) ?? (await client.GetFoldersAsync(...)).FirstOrDefault(f => f.Name.Equals("Sent", ...));` sits inside a `catch (Exception ex)` that only logs a warning. MailKit's GetFolder(SpecialFolder) throws NotSupportedException when the server does not advertise special-use folders, so the `??` fallback only runs when the capability exists.

The change adds four third-party dependencies: the HtmlSanitizer NuGet package, and Quill, marked and Turndown loaded at runtime from jsDelivr with no Subresource Integrity hashes. A compromised CDN response would run in the authenticated app. `<PackageReference Include="HtmlSanitizer" Version="9.0.892" />`. index.html adds `<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/quill@2.0.3/dist/quill.js">`, plus `marked@15.0.7` and `turndown@7.2.0`, all without `integrity=` or `crossorigin=` attributes.

The outgoing-HTML sanitizer explicitly allows the `data:` URI scheme. Links in sent mail can then carry `data:text/html` payloads, which spam filters and some recipient clients treat as phishing indicators. `sanitizer.AllowedSchemes.Add("data");` applies to all URL attributes, including `href`, not just image sources.

The `ComposeValidationMailbox` key (in all 4 Web resx files) and the `SendMailFailed` key (in all 4 Api resx files) are never referenced. `quillInterop.getText` and `destroy` (which only nulls the reference) are unused or ineffective. `IsValidEmail` is copied word for word in Compose.razor and ComposeEndpoints.cs instead of being shared from Feirb.Shared.

When an admin edits a source URL that already has a token and doesn't retype it, the token is silently dropped instead of moving to the new URL, so syncing a private repo starts failing. On rename, McpServerGitSync.svelte:162-171 deletes the old key and sends `sourceURLCredentials[newUrl] = '*'`. In Update, the '*' case only does `if tok, ok := existingCred.Env[u]; ok`, with u being the new URL. The stored credential is keyed by the old URL, so nothing is copied, and the old URL is not in activeURLs, so its token is discarded. The comment 'transferred from a renamed one' describes behaviour the code doesn't have. Trigger: edit https://github.com/org/private-repo to https://github.com/org/private-repo/other-branch and save with the token field empty. newTokens comes out empty, DeleteCredential runs, and the next sync clones without auth.

A token entered together with a URL that has no scheme is silently thrown away, because the URL is given an https:// prefix but the key in the credentials map is not. Lines 156-158 rewrite `manifest.SourceURLs[i] = "https://" + urlStr`, but `manifest.SourceURLCredentials` keeps the raw key the UI sent (`[editingSource.value]: editingSource.token`). At line 185 `if _, active := activeURLs[u]; !active { continue }` then skips it. Trigger: add `github.com/org/private` with a PAT. The URL is saved with no credential, the response shows no '*', and no error is returned.

Existing deployments that rely on GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN for a private GitHub catalog, including a custom default catalog set through OBOT_SERVER_DEFAULT_MCPCATALOG_PATH, lose authentication on upgrade and their syncs start failing. Before the change, `githubToken` was applied to every github.com clone and size check. `resolveToken` now returns the env token only when `catalogURL == defaultCatalogURL`, a hardcoded "https://github.com/obot-platform/mcp-catalog". It is not compared with the configured `defaultCatalogPath` (Dockerfile:61 sets it through an env var that operators can override). Every other GitHub URL now clones and calls the API without auth. Size checks on public repos also become unauthenticated, so they hit GitHub's lower rate limit. No migration or release note covers this.

Raw catalog file URLs on gitlab.com used to be fetched as raw files and now fail to sync. `isGitRepoURL` now returns true for any `gitlab.com` host. For `https://gitlab.com/org/repo/-/raw/main/catalog.yaml`, `parseGitURL` finds no `.git` segment and falls into the gitlab.com branch, which sets the branch to `-/raw/main/catalog.yaml`. `validateBranchName` rejects that because of `strings.HasPrefix(branch, "-")`. Before the change, `isGitHubURL` was false for gitlab.com, so the URL went down the raw-file HTTP GET path.

The size limit applied during clone may reject repositories well under 100 MB, because it adds up the packfile in .git and the checked-out working tree against the same budget. A single `sizeLimitedFS` (maxBytes = 100 MiB) is both the worktree filesystem and, through `chroot.New(limitedFS, ".git")`, the object storage passed to `git.CloneContext`. Every Write to the pack, the index and the checked-out files adds to one shared counter (`f.fs.written.Add`). A repo whose pack plus checkout is over 100 MiB fails with 'repository is too large', even though checkGitHubRepoSize, which uses the API repo size, passed it.

The catalog's URL list is saved before the credential is written, so if the credential write fails the user gets an error even though the URL change has already been applied, without its token. `req.Update(&catalog)` runs at line 197. `CreateCredential` or `DeleteCredential` only runs afterwards (lines 202-218), and a failure there returns an error with nothing rolled back.

Listing or getting catalogs now fails completely if the credential store returns an error other than not-found, even though the only thing it adds is a '*' presence marker. `revealCatalogTokens` returns any non-NotFound error, and List/Get do `if err != nil { return err }` for each catalog. List also makes one RevealCredential call per catalog on every request.

The rules for merging tokens in Update (keep with '*', clear with '', replace, drop for removed URLs) have no tests, which is how the rename and scheme-normalisation defects got through. The diff adds tests only for isGitRepoURL, parseGitURL, readGitCatalog and sizeLimitedFS. No test exercises `MCPCatalogHandler.Update` or `convertMCPCatalog` masking.

TestReadGitCatalog clones live GitHub repositories, so its result depends on network access and the state of an external repo. The test calls `readGitCatalog(context.Background(), "https://github.com/obot-platform/test-mcp-catalog.git", "")`, and the new case does a real clone.

The change modifies the DeleteCredential handler, which the story doesn't cover: a not-found error now returns success. The target changed from `(*gptscript.ErrNotFound)(nil)` to `gptscript.ErrNotFound{}`. The download directory is built from the remote manifest's `name` without any check, so a malicious skillset can make `spm install` write files anywhere the user can write (for example under their home directory), not just under the temp folder. `const tmpDir = join(tmpdir(), 'spm', skillset.name)`. `skillset.name` comes from `fetchSkillset`/`validateSkillset`, which only check that it is a string. `join` resolves `..`, so `name: "../../../../../../../../home/victim"` points tmpDir outside the temp folder. `safePath(tmpDir, result.path)` then checks paths against that already-escaped base, so it allows writes such as a `setup: ../../.bashrc` entry (path `claude/fsd/../../.bashrc`, which normalizes to `.bashrc`) to land at `/home/victim/.bashrc` through `writeFile`.

The path-traversal guard is a plain string-prefix check, so a path can escape into a sibling directory whose name starts with the skillset name. `if (!resolved.startsWith(baseDir))` does not require a path separator after the base. With baseDir `/tmp/spm/fsd`, a file entry `../fsd-evil/x` resolves to `/tmp/spm/fsd-evil/x`, and `startsWith('/tmp/spm/fsd')` is true, so the write goes ahead outside the intended folder. It should compare against `baseDir + sep` or use `path.relative`.

GitHub tree URLs throw away the branch, so `spm install https://github.com/org/repo/tree/develop/path` installs from the repo's default branch instead of `develop`, or fails with a 404 when the path exists only on that branch. The regex `/^https?:\/\/github\.com\/([^/]+)\/([^/]+)\/tree\/[^/]+\/(.+)$/` does not capture the branch segment, and `SkillIdentifier` has no ref field. `resolveIdentifier` always sets `ref` from `fetchDefaultBranch(...)`. The test 'parses GitHub URL with non-main branch' only checks owner, repo and path, so it passes even though the branch is lost. Branch names containing a slash (`feature/x`) are also parsed wrong: `x/...` becomes part of the path.

The new `..` check covers only bare sources. `./` sources, `@` cross-repo sources, `setup`, the `files` entries and the agents/hooks/mcp/memory/rules lists still accept `..`, so a manifest can still point paths outside its folder. Only the fallback branch runs `normalized.includes('..')`. The `./` branch builds `${skillsetDir}/${relativePath}` unchecked, `files.forEach` appends `${resolved.basePath}/${file}` unchecked, and `setup` and the local file types are concatenated straight onto `skillsetDir`. Those paths reach `downloadFromGitHub` and `safePath` unchanged.

Files from earlier installs are never cleaned up, and a failed run leaves a partly written folder, so the 'Downloaded N file(s)' location can hold stale or mixed content from different runs. `tmpDir` is a fixed path, `join(tmpdir(), 'spm', skillset.name)`. It is never cleared or created fresh with `mkdtemp`. Writes run concurrently in `Promise.all` and are not rolled back if one of them fails, and the same goes for downloads in `downloadEntries`.

The version test went from pinning the exact value to checking only its shape, so it would pass if the `__VERSION__` define were wrong or stale. `expect(stdout.trim()).toBe('0.1.0')` became `toMatch(/^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/)`. The test is not compared against `package.json`'s `version`.

The install integration test checks only that a 'Resolving' message was printed. It never checks what actually happens: here the `test-skillset` input is rejected, and nothing is written to disk. `expect(stdout).toContain('Resolving test-skillset')`. With this input `parseIdentifier` throws 'Must start with @', which goes to stderr, and the test never checks the exit code or the files on disk.

An existing test that rejected unrecognised skill sources was replaced by one that expects them to be accepted. Every bare string now becomes a repo-root path, and the packet records no story decision for that change. The diff removes `it('throws on invalid skill source format'...)` and adds `it('resolves bare path as repo-root relative'...)`. `resolveSkillSource` no longer throws 'Invalid skill source' for unknown formats.

The package version was bumped to 0.2.0 inside a feature change. `vite.config.ts` now imports `package.json` to inject `__VERSION__`, so release versioning is now tied to the build config, and the packet shows no request for either change. `"version": "0.1.0"` → `"0.2.0"`. `vite.config.ts` adds `import { version } from './package.json'` and `define: { __VERSION__: JSON.stringify(version) }`. `src/bin/spm.ts` uses `declare const __VERSION__`. The mounted config (backend/ai-secure-agent-config.yaml:14) sets `username: "root"` for MySQL with no password. Every other service in the repo gets its password from the secret env. The new Argo CD Application deploys from the feature branch `AI-20-AISecureAgent-Feature-collection` with automated prune and selfHeal. The live cluster will follow an unmerged branch: any push to it deploys straight away, and deleting or merging the branch breaks the app's sync. `targetRevision: AI-20-AISecureAgent-Feature-collection` together with `syncPolicy: automated: prune: true, selfHeal: true`. Every other in-repo Application and the helm-app ApplicationSet use `targetRevision: HEAD` / `revision: HEAD` (e.g. lines 10, 77, 100, 111, 137). The migration drops the liveness and readiness probes. Kubernetes will route traffic to the agent before it is ready, and will never restart it if it hangs. The deleted helm_backend/ai-secure-agent-ms/values.yaml defined `livenessProbe`/`readinessProbe` on `/ai-secure-agent-ms/v1/ping` (10s delay, 5s period), and the chart rendered both (charts/templates/deployment.yaml:55-68). The new container spec (lines 25-46) has no `livenessProbe` or `readinessProbe`.

The container's CPU and memory requests and limits are removed. The agent, which already needed a 345Mi cap and MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 to tame memory, can now use unbounded node memory, and the scheduler gives it no reservation. The old values had `requests: cpu 100m, memory 256Mi` and `limits: cpu 200m, memory 345Mi`, rendered at charts/templates/deployment.yaml:69-75. The new container spec has no `resources:` block. The change keeps `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX: "2"` (lines 40-41), which shows memory was a known concern.

Moving the same Deployment and Service names from the helm-app ApplicationSet to the new agent-app may leave two Argo CD apps owning, then pruning, the same resources during the cutover. That could cause downtime or a delete-and-recreate. The deleted helm_backend/ai-secure-agent-ms/values.yaml removes the `helm_backend/*` directory entry, so the ApplicationSet (app-of-apps.yaml:96-125, automated prune) drops the `ai-secure-agent-ms` Application. Meanwhile agent-app (`name: agent-app`) creates a Deployment named `ai-secure-agent-ms` and a Service `ai-secure-agent-ms-svc`, the same names the chart produced from `{{ .Release.Name }}` / `{{ .Release.Name }}-svc`. Nothing in the diff orders or coordinates the handover. Also, the ApplicationSet watches `revision: HEAD` while agent-app watches the feature branch, so until merge both may run at once.

Copying the Deployment out of the shared Helm chart into raw YAML duplicates the chart's job. This one service now drifts from the conventions every other microservice gets: anti-affinity, the HPA, the secret env and probes. All other services (helm_backend/*/values.yaml) render through charts/templates/deployment.yaml, which supplies podAntiAffinity, envFrom, probes, resources and the hpa.tpl. agent/ai-secure-agent.yaml re-implements a subset by hand. Its ConfigMap stays in backend/ai-secure-agent-config.yaml under a different Argo app (backend-app), which splits one service across two apps.

In cluster mode without --server-url, the CLI connects to the operator's in-cluster service DNS name. That name doesn't resolve from a workstation, so the documented primary invocation fails for anyone running outside the cluster. resolveURL returns status.endpoints.admin first. Its own comment says "the toolkit runs outside the cluster", but the operator sets that endpoint in keycloak_reconciler.py:465 to `http://{name}-keycloak.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local:8080`, and public is the same in-cluster URL. Every example in docs/how-to/migration-toolkit.md and export-realms.md uses `--keycloak … --namespace …` with no --server-url and says "Credentials are resolved automatically from the cluster". authenticate() then POSTs to `http://x-keycloak.ns.svc.cluster.local:8080/realms/master/...` and fails DNS resolution.

decodeSecretKey decodes the secret value a second time whenever it looks like base64. About 1 in 7 operator-generated admin passwords get decoded into garbage, so cluster-mode authentication fails with a 401. client-go already returns decoded Secret.Data. The code then runs `if isBase64(decoded) { base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString(decoded) … return string(b) }`. isBase64 accepts any string whose length is a multiple of 4 and that uses only [A-Za-z0-9+/=]. The operator generates passwords as 16 characters from letters+digits+"!@#$%^&*" (utils/kubernetes.py:1428-1429), so (62/70)^16 ≈ 14% of them are 16 alphanumeric characters. Those pass isBase64, decode successfully to 12 random bytes, and get sent as the password. A user-chosen existingSecret password such as "Password1234" is mangled the same way. The operator's own reconciler decodes only once (keycloak_reconciler.py:1315-1320).

The hard-failure check on `errors > 0`, and the error-detail collection, may rely on response fields and action values that Keycloak's Partial Import response doesn't contain. If so, the check never fires, and OVERWRITE results go uncounted. importResp parses `errors` and collects results whose Action is "ERROR" or "FAILED" (line 217). Keycloak's PartialImportResults reports added/skipped/overwritten, with result actions ADDED/SKIPPED/OVERWRITTEN; failures come back as non-200 HTTP. `overwritten` isn't parsed at all, so an OVERWRITE run prints Added 0 / Skipped 0. No test exercises importBatch against a real or recorded response.

When a batch fails at the HTTP level (409 in FAIL mode, 5xx, 403, network error), ImportUsers returns a nil result. The user never sees how many users earlier batches already committed, even though those batches aren't rolled back. `batchResult, err := importBatch(...); if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("batch %d/%d failed: %w", ...) }`. In cmd/import_users.go:162 the comment says "Print partial result before returning error so user can see progress", but printImportSummary returns immediately when result == nil. The partial result is printed only on the `errors > 0` path, which may never fire (see the previous finding).

Every HTTP call goes through http.DefaultClient, which has no timeout, so an unresponsive Keycloak or proxy hangs the import indefinitely. authenticate and importBatch (line 174) both call `http.DefaultClient.Do(req)`. ctx is `context.Background()` in runImportUsers with no deadline. The decision record says batching exists to avoid timeouts, but no client-side timeout is set.

The new auth and credential-handling code has no tests. Only chunk() and LoadUsersFile are covered, which is how both high-severity defects above went uncaught. The test files contain only TestChunk_* and TestLoadUsersFile_*. Nothing tests authenticate, token refresh, importBatch response parsing or errors>0 failure, ResolveFromCluster, resolveURL, decodeSecretKey/isBase64, ResolveFromFlags, parseImportMode, or the credential-mode selection in runImportUsers. An httptest server and a fake dynamic/core client would cover them.

The admin password is accepted only as a --password argument, which exposes it in the process list and in shell or CI history. The docs recommend this path for CI. `f.StringVar(&importUsersOpts.password, "password", "", ...)`. There is no environment-variable or stdin alternative. The docs' CI example passes `--password "$KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD"`, which still puts the expanded master-realm admin password on argv, visible via ps or /proc while the import runs.

The change pulls in the full k8s client-go tree as unvetted new dependencies, and some indirect versions may carry known advisories. go.mod adds k8s.io/client-go v0.32.3 and k8s.io/apimachinery v0.32.3 plus about 35 indirect modules, including golang.org/x/net v0.30.0 and golang.org/x/oauth2 v0.23.0, versions that predate published Go vulnerability fixes. risk.json lists `dependency` as unplanned with gate:deps required. The only justification is the ADR written in this same change (provenance: guided-ai), and the packet shows no govulncheck or provenance record.

The spec.hostname fallback in resolveURL is dead code, because the Keycloak CR has no top-level spec.hostname field. KeycloakSpec maps `Hostname string json:"hostname"`. In the operator model (models/keycloak.py), hostname exists only under spec.tls (KeycloakTLSConfig.hostname, line 56) and the ingress config, so kc.Spec.Hostname is always empty and the scheme/hostname branch in kubeclient.go never runs.

When both --keycloak and --username/--password are passed, the code silently ignores --keycloak instead of rejecting the ambiguous call. The docs say "Exactly one mode must be chosen". `usingExplicitCreds := importUsersOpts.username != "" || importUsersOpts.password != ""` picks the flags path and never checks keycloakName. migration-toolkit.md says "Exactly one mode must be chosen".

The stale-export guard relies on file mtime, so a plain copy or checkout of an old users.json resets its age and passes the check. `fileAge := time.Since(info.ModTime())`. `cp` without -p or a git checkout gives an old export a fresh mtime. The file has no export timestamp to check against.

The new Go files aren't gofmt-formatted, which may fail a formatting gate. Field alignment in the anonymous Results struct is inconsistent (`Action      string` next to `ResourceType string`), and types.go has `Endpoints KeycloakEndpoints  ` with trailing misalignment. gofmt would rewrite both.
